tweets: Let's talk about risk-to-reward optimization. 🧵
Brutal truth: risk-to-reward isn't just about aiming for 3:1. It's about optimization.

Tighter entries = better R:R. Wider stops with higher targets = better probability. Partial exits = guaranteed partial R:R. The best setups balance probability of hitting target against the reward offered.

Minimum 2:1 R:R before entering. No exceptions.

Optimization in practice: if your planned stop is 30 pips and the target is 40, that's 1:1.3. Can you tighten the entry to get a 20-pip stop? Now it's 1:2. Same trade, better entry, better math.

Wait for a close above the level before entering.

Common mistake: fixating on a minimum R:R ratio and passing on every trade that doesn't meet it. A high-probability 1:1.5 setup taken consistently can outperform a low-probability 1:3 setup over 200 trades.

tweets: Where you put your stop matters as much as where you enter. Maybe more. 🧵

Behind structure (safest). ATR-based (volatility-adjusted). Fixed distance (simplest). Below order block (smart money). Your stop should be at the level that invalidates your thesis — not where it feels comfortable.

Real application: for an ATR-based stop, take the 14-period ATR and multiply by 1.5. That gives you a volatility-adjusted distance. In quiet markets, your stop is tight. In volatile markets, it widens to avoid noise. Bookmark this.

Pro tip: combine structure-based and ATR-based stops. Place your stop behind the key structural level, but verify it's at least 1 ATR away from entry. If it's not, either widen the stop or reduce position size.

The relationship between stop distance and position size is non-negotiable. Wider stop = smaller position. Tighter stop = larger position. The dollar risk stays constant. If you widen the stop without reducing size, you've just doubled your risk.

Test your stop placement: review your last 20 stopped-out trades. Were you stopped by noise (price hit your stop then reversed)? If more than 30% were noise stops, your placement needs adjustment. The data tells you whether your stops are in the right place.

title: 📝 The Sunk Cost Fallacy in Trading

tweets: I spent years and thousands on courses before building something better. Free. 🧵
"I've already lost so much, I can't exit now." That's the sunk cost fallacy talking.

What you've lost is gone. The only question: with fresh eyes, would you open this position right now? If the answer is no, the position should be closed. Past losses don't justify future ones.

(I wish I was joking. I'm not.)
Ask yourself this question every day about every open position: "If I had no position right now, would I enter this trade at this price, at this size?" If no, the only logical action is to close it.
The sunk cost fallacy isn't about money. It's about ego. Closing a loser means admitting you were wrong. But being wrong and adapting quickly is how professionals operate. Ego is the real enemy here.

Practice this: at the start of each day, look at every open position as if you just discovered it. Would you open it fresh right now? If not, close it. This daily reset breaks the emotional grip that past decisions have on your present judgment.

The costs you don't see eating your profits.

→ High volatility periods
→ News events

→ Avoid news-heavy periods

tweets: Let's talk about the importance of liquidity. 🧵
Liquidity determines how easily you can enter and exit. It's not optional to understand.

High liquidity: tight spreads, easy fills, low slippage. Low liquidity: wide spreads, partial fills, high slippage. Trade liquid markets. Avoid illiquid ones unless you know exactly what you're doing.

Practical rule: check the bid-ask spread before entering any trade. If the spread is more than 5% of your stop distance, the trade is too expensive. On a 20-pip stop, the spread should be under 1 pip.

Mistake: trading exotic pairs or low-cap altcoins with tight stops. Low liquidity means wide spreads and slippage that can eat your edge entirely. Stick to liquid markets until your account size demands otherwise.

Time-of-day matters for liquidity. The same pair has different liquidity at London open vs Tokyo close. Trade during the session with the deepest liquidity for your market. For forex, that's London-NY overlap. For crypto, it's US business hours.

Liquidity also affects indicator accuracy. Indicators based on price and volume are more reliable in liquid markets. In illiquid markets, erratic price moves create false signals. Filter your setups by liquidity before trusting the reading.

tweets: Let's talk about trading plan essentials. 🧵
A trading plan answers four questions: What, when, how, and how much.
Strategy rules. Risk parameters. Entry/exit criteria. Position sizing formula. Review schedule. If any of these are missing, your plan has a hole. Holes leak money. Fill them before you trade.

A minimal trading plan on one page: market (what), session (when), setup + trigger (how I enter), stop + target (how I exit), 1% max risk (how much), journal review Sunday (how I improve). One page. Done.

Common mistake: writing a 20-page plan you never look at. A plan that lives in a drawer is no plan at all. Keep it short enough to read in 2 minutes. Tape it next to your monitor. Review it before every session.

Update your plan quarterly. Markets evolve, your skills improve, and what worked six months ago might need adjustment. A living plan that adapts is worth ten static plans collecting dust in a folder somewhere.

tweets: Let's talk about reading order flow simply. 🧵

RSI at 70 doesn't mean overbought. In trends, it means strong.

Order flow sounds complex. The basics aren't. Here's the simplified version.

More buying than selling = price goes up. More selling than buying = price goes down. Volume at key levels = strong conviction. Low volume at key levels = weak conviction. Start there.

(Fun fact: the traders who ignore this are the same ones who complain about the market.)

Exercise: pick one key level and watch volume every time price touches it. If volume spikes and price bounces, that's demand. If volume spikes and price breaks, that's a liquidation event. Volume at levels is the simplest flow reading.

Mistake: overcomplicating order flow with tools you don't understand. Footprint charts and delta analysis are powerful but unnecessary for beginners. Master volume bars at key levels first. Add complexity later when the basics are second nature.

tweets: A candle without context is just a shape on a screen. 🧵
Wicks tell stories that candle bodies don't. Learn to read them.

Long lower wick = buyers stepped in with force. Long upper wick = sellers rejected the high. Both wicks = indecision. No wicks = pure dominance. The wick is the rejected narrative. The body is the accepted one.

Next time you see a long lower wick at support: that wick represents every seller who tried to push price down and failed. The buyers at the bottom of that wick are telling you something. Listen to the rejection.

Mistake: ignoring wicks on higher timeframes. A weekly candle with a 3% lower wick at a key support level is a major signal. Daily and intraday wicks can be noise, but weekly and monthly wicks carry real institutional weight.

Wicks are footprints of the battle between buyers and sellers.

The breakout trap: price breaks above resistance with a strong candle. You buy the breakout. Volume on the breakout bar is below average. Price immediately reverses and sweeps your stop. You just provided exit liquidity for the traders who were already long below the level.

Three breakout confirmation filters:

1. Volume surge — breakout on declining volume is suspect
2. Retest — price breaks, pulls back, holds the level as new support
3. Multi-timeframe agreement — breakout on 1H confirmed by 4H direction

The false breakout: price breaks resistance, triggers retail buys, reverses back below. Your stop gets hit. Smart money used your entry as their exit. Wait for the retest. Let others be the liquidity.

How to use leverage responsibly:

1. Calculate position size FIRST (based on 1-2% risk)

3. Never let leverage determine your position size

Leverage is a tool for capital efficiency, not for amplifying gambles.

The rule: if your position size would be the same without leverage, you're using it correctly. If leverage is making you take bigger positions than you can afford to lose, you're using it as a casino chip.

The revenge trade is trading's most expensive therapy session.
The revenge trade pattern: lose $200 on a clean setup. Feel the sting. Open a new chart. Enter without a plan, with double the position size, within 5 minutes. Lose $400 more.

After a losing streak, the protocol:

1. Close the platform immediately
2. Review: bad process or bad luck?
3. Bad process — fix the system before trading again
4. Bad luck — your edge is intact. Size down and continue.

The size-down rule: after 3 consecutive losses, cut position size by 50% for the next 5 trades. This limits damage during cold streaks while keeping you in the game. If those 5 trades are profitable, return to normal size. Mechanical. No emotion.

title: Pre-Trade Routines: Removing Emotion Before the Session

tweets: The hardest part of trading has nothing to do with charts. 🧵
A pre-trade routine removes emotion from the equation before the session starts. By the time price is moving, your decisions are already made. You're executing, not deciding.

The 15-min pre-trade routine:

1. Check daily chart — trend? (2 min)
2. Mark 3 key levels on 4H (3 min)
3. Write scenarios: "If X, I do Y" (5 min)
4. Set alerts at key levels (3 min)
5. Walk away until alerted (2 min)

Total: 15 minutes of prep. Hours of freedom.
Try this: before your next trade, write down your emotional state. Just one word. Review it after the trade closes.
